rationale: Both designs are sound and share the core ideas: protect the interactive class, treat the swap as the dominant cost, use hysteresis against thrash, a tiered session cache and a VRAM ledger. A has some good specifics: offloading KV to CPU RAM on swap-out, a reserved interactive KV slice, reconciling the ledger against the allocator, and asking the user to confirm an ambiguous swap. B is more concrete and actionable where the prompt asks most. It has an explicit router state machine with a deadline on every transition, a quantified admission rule and swap-feasibility check, a page-cache hot standby to make loads cheaper, and a real engine constraint (per-sequence abort within a batch). Its failure-mode section is the more insightful one: it targets silent failures with a post-load canary prompt, model content hashes to invalidate stale session caches, a heartbeat watchdog for GPU hangs, and swap-deadlock timeouts, and it backs these with a concrete metrics list. B's weaknesses are a muddled swap decision pseudocode and simply discarding KV on swap, where A's offload is better. Still, its operational depth and instrumentation-first framing give it the edge.
